description: Somos un grupo de joveens comprometidos con el desarrollo de iniciativas que impulsen el uso de los datos de la NASA
summary:
ORBITAL Shield is a bilingual 3D educational game built by Apolo 3730 for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players design a spacecraft, pass a flight readiness review, launch, and make decisions when problems arise in flight. Every component affects what the spacecraft can do within its mass, budget, power, and communications limits.

The game offers three missions: Earth Observer, a satellite mission to study Earth from orbit; Ritmo Quisqueya, a simulated orbital broadcast of Dominican music; and Selene, a crewed mission to lunar orbit. Designed for students, educators, and curious players, ORBITAL Shield makes engineering trade-offs tangible. Players can see why a design passes or fails, then use their flight report to improve it.
details:
Players begin by choosing a mission and receiving a briefing from Mission Control. In the 3D workshop, they assemble a spacecraft and see how each component affects mass, cost, power, storage, and communications. A flight readiness review gives them a GO or NO-GO decision and explains which requirements they need to meet before launch.

Each mission rewards different choices. Earth Observer asks players to balance scientific instruments, pointing accuracy, and data downlink. Ritmo Quisqueya draws on the student-built TJ3Sat to turn a communications mission into a celebration of Dominican music. Selene adds crew-specific requirements such as a pressurized capsule, life support, deep-space communications, and thermal protection. Players can follow the spacecraft along a simplified Earth–Moon trajectory and watch the camera close in as it enters lunar orbit.

After launch, players monitor telemetry and respond to anomalies. Their flight report shows how the design and their decisions affected the outcome. The game runs in a web browser, supports English and Spanish, and uses mission briefings and guided workshop tasks to help first-time players get started.

The team used React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Zustand, and Lucide. Blender was used to prepare 3D assets in GLB format. Component specifications, flight telemetry, and mission outcomes use simplified models designed for learning.
